hops.afterHeading: Start at the skin: one sensation, several inputs
hops.title: Why pre-workout powder makes your skin itch
hops.text: Pre-workout powders that contain beta-alanine can leave your skin tingling and itchy. Athletes take beta-alanine, an amino acid, to raise muscle carnosine and buffer acid during high-intensity exercise. In 2012, researchers found that in mice beta-alanine-evoked scratching drops sharply without MrgprD, a receptor on skin-innervating sensory neurons that did not respond to histamine in those tests. When people received beta-alanine in the skin, they felt itch with no wheal or flare—no raised bump and no surrounding redness. That skin response gave researchers a clue that beta-alanine can make people itch through a histamine-independent route.

sources.citation: Liu et al., Journal of Neuroscience, 2012 (PMID 23077038)

image.alt: AI-generated illustration: A gym shaker bottle and scoop of powder on a locker-room bench next to a student seen from behind scratching an arm.
image.caption: Skin-injected beta-alanine causes itch without wheal or flare in people, and MrgprD-dependent scratching in mice.

hops.afterHeading: Mechanical itch: a partly separate route
hops.title: How vibrating fine facial hairs evokes itch
hops.text: The next time a stray strand of hair brushes your cheek, notice whether it feels itchy, ticklish, or simply like touch. In a 2013 Kyoto University study, gently vibrating fine hairs with a device evoked intense itch on the face but not on the arm, and during a 10-minute stimulation trial the itch peaked within 10 seconds. The itch produced no flare, was not described as burning or stinging, and resisted H1 blockers. After 90 seconds of vibration, it took more than 10 minutes to fade completely, while light touch also evoked itch—alloknesis—in adjacent skin.

image.alt: AI-generated illustration: A student near an open window pausing as a breeze blows a stray strand of hair across one cheek.
image.caption: Vibrating fine facial hairs evoked itch without flare or burning and resisted H1 blockers, with adjacent alloknesis.

hops.afterHeading: Into the spinal cord: the relay and its brakes
hops.title: The link between a toad-skin peptide and a spinal itch receptor
hops.text: In 1971, researchers isolated a 14-amino-acid peptide from the skin of the European fire-bellied toad, Bombina bombina, and named it bombesin. In 1982, Gmerek and Cowan reported that delivering bombesin into fluid-filled spaces inside a rat's brain caused dose-related excessive grooming, and the same authors asked in a 1983 note whether bombesin might be a central mediator of itch. Mammals make a related peptide, GRP. When Sun and Chen tested GRPR-mutant mice in 2007, pain responses stayed comparable while scratching to pruritogens fell significantly, linking the bombesin family to spinal itch signalling.

audio.title: A mouse cheek test, a toad-skin peptide, and itchy dogs
audio.transcript:
Here are three true stories about how researchers untangled the biology of itch, starting with a surprisingly tricky measurement problem in mice.

In the standard mouse itch test, researchers injected a compound into the back of the neck and counted hind-paw scratches. That seemed straightforward, except researchers could not be certain whether the mouse was actually itchy or simply in pain. In two thousand eight, Shimada and LaMotte at Yale showed why. When they injected histamine into the back of a mouse's neck, the mouse scratched with its hind paw. When they injected capsaicin—the burning compound known to evoke predominantly pain in people—into that same neck spot, the mouse still scratched with its hind paw. At the nape, only one site-directed behavior, hind-paw scratching, is available. So Shimada and LaMotte moved the injection forward to the mouse's cheek. At the cheek, the behaviors separated: histamine mainly brought up the hind paw to scratch, while capsaicin mainly brought up the front paw to wipe. Shifting from the neck to the cheek gave researchers a much clearer way to separate itch-related from pain-related behavior.

Once you can tell those behaviors apart, the next puzzle is how an itch signal moves through the spinal cord. One unlikely clue began with an amphibian. Back in nineteen seventy-one, researchers isolated a fourteen-amino-acid peptide from the skin of the European fire-bellied toad, Bombina bombina, and named it bombesin. Eleven years later, a team reported that delivering bombesin into fluid-filled spaces inside a rat's brain caused dose-related excessive grooming, and the same authors asked in a nineteen eighty-three note whether bombesin might be a central mediator of itch. Mammals make a related peptide called gastrin-releasing peptide, or G R P. In two thousand seven, Sun and Chen found the G R P receptor, G R P R, in the dorsal spinal cord and tested mice with a mutation in its gene. Those mice reacted comparably to wild-type mice on thermal, mechanical, inflammatory, and neuropathic pain tests, while their scratching to itch-producing chemicals fell significantly. G R P R, a receptor for a mammalian relative of that toad peptide, was proposed in two thousand seven as the first spinal receptor dedicated to itch.

Our last story moves to the immune system, and to the veterinary clinic. In two thousand thirteen, researchers found quantifiable levels of the immune cytokine I L thirty-one in fifty-seven percent of dogs with naturally occurring atopic dermatitis, while the assay could not reliably quantify it in serum from the healthy dogs they tested. In two thousand seventeen, European regulators authorized lokivetmab, the first monoclonal antibody recommended for veterinary medicine in the European Union. In a laboratory onset experiment with beagles, lokivetmab reduced I L thirty-one-induced itch behavior during the first observation window, three to four hours after treatment. In a separate duration experiment with another group of beagles, first assessed one day after treatment, the highest dose tested reduced itch behavior compared with placebo at day forty-two. A human antibody blocking I L thirty-one receptor alpha, nemolizumab, was first approved in Japan in two thousand twenty-two, and by the U S F D A in August two thousand twenty-four. For antibodies targeting the I L thirty-one pathway, dogs really did go first: lokivetmab binds the canine cytokine itself, while nemolizumab blocks the human receptor.
